newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish bourse set to expand, eyes more investors.
newsitem.headline: Polish bourse set to expand, eyes more investors.

text.p: Poland's fledgling stock market is set to grow in size and open up further next year, which will probably attract more foreign investors, Polish officials told an international conference on Thursday.

Bourse president Wieslaw Rozlucki, speaking at a two-day International Herald Tribune investment forum, said next year's flotations of Poland's copper giant KGHM and leading commercial bank Bank Handlowy woud boost the market's capitalisation.

Rozlucki said expansion of the Warsaw market should especially help attract foreign investors, who now have about a 25-percent share of the market and have pointed to its relatively small size as the main barrier to larger investment.

"I have been hearing from foreign investors that they would like to come to Poland but that there is not enough to buy, so my message is: keep your wallets ready because the supply is coming," Rozlucki said.

He later told Reuters he expected foreign investors could double their investment within three to four years and the market capitalisation could grow to 20 percent of gross domestic product from the current seven percent in five years.
He said the Warsaw bourse was seen as attractive because it was promising higher returns than Western exchanges while offering a similar level of safety and the same legal standards.

But Wolfgang Bauer, chief executive of Creditanstalt Securities SA, the Polish securities subsidiary of Austria's Creditanstalt Bankverein AG, said Poland had yet to remove several barriers to investment.

He said pre-payment for shares, freezing funds before their allocation, a lack of derivatives which made risk management and hedging difficult and a lack of clear rules in allotment of new share issues were cooling some investor enthusiasm for Polish stocks.

The Polish Securities Commission Chairman Jacek Socha said a new securities trading law, now in parliament and expected to come into force early in 1997, would make the Polish market more accessible to foreign players.

The law would allow foreign companies to raise capital through new share offerings and debt issues in Poland, would create a legal framework for derivatives trading and liberalise access of foreign brokers and advisers to the Polish market.
